#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Complementation as a Free Involution on Framed-Puzzle Assembly Spaces
=====================================================================

Numerical demonstration of the results on global tab-blank complementation.

MODEL
-----
A *framed puzzle* on n variables is a finite list of *clause pieces*.  A clause
piece is a list of *literal inputs* (notches), each a pair (i, p) with
i in {0,...,n-1} a variable index and p in {True, False} the polarity the notch
is milled for.  An *assembly* is a point a of the Boolean cube {0,1}^n: for each
variable you install either its true piece or its false piece.

  * The notch (i, p) fits under a  <=>  a[i] == p.
  * A clause piece snaps into place under a  <=>  some notch of it fits.
  * a assembles P  <=>  every clause piece of P snaps into place.

The assembly space A(P) is the set of all assemblies of P.

Global complementation re-mills every notch for the opposite polarity:
    P*  =  [[(i, not p) for (i, p) in c] for c in P],
and on assemblies it is Boolean negation  sigma(a)[i] = not a[i].

RESULTS DEMONSTRATED
--------------------
1.  Exact transport:            A(P*) = sigma(A(P)),   |A(P*)| = |A(P)|.
2.  Untagged parity:            |A(P) u A(P*)| is even for n >= 1.
3.  Self-dual parity:           a complement-stable assembly space has even size.
4.  Sharpness at n = 0:         the combined count is 1 -- odd.
5.  Orbit decomposition:        |S| = 2 |Gauge(S)| for complement-stable S.
6.  Sign of complementation:    sgn(sigma) = (-1)^(2^(n-1)); odd iff n = 1.
7.  Complete expressiveness:    every subset of the cube is an assembly space,
                                realised with 2^n - |S| clause pieces.
8.  Combined spectrum:          achievable combined counts on n >= 1 variables
                                are exactly the even numbers <= 2^n.
9.  Density of self-duality:    exactly 2^(2^(n-1)) complement-stable spaces,
                                the square root of the total 2^(2^n).
10. Cyclic divisibility:        with d interlock depths, d divides the combined
                                count over all d depth shifts.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Types
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Assembly = Tuple[bool, ...]            # a point of the Boolean cube {T,F}^n
Notch = Tuple[int, bool]               # (variable index, milled polarity)
ClausePiece = List[Notch]              # one clause piece
FramedPuzzle = List[ClausePiece]       # a framed puzzle on n variables

DAssembly = Tuple[int, ...]            # a point of (Z/d)^n
DNotch = Tuple[int, int]               # (variable index, milled depth)
DClausePiece = List[DNotch]
DFramedPuzzle = List[DClausePiece]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The Boolean framed-puzzle model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def cube(n: int) -> List[Assembly]:
    """All 2^n assemblies of the Boolean cube, in lexicographic order."""
    return [tuple(bits) for bits in itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n)]


def notch_fits(a: Assembly, notch: Notch) -> bool:
    """The local dictionary: the notch (i,p) interlocks under a iff a[i] == p."""
    i, p = notch
    return a[i] == p


def piece_snaps(a: Assembly, piece: ClausePiece) -> bool:
    """A clause piece snaps into place iff at least one of its notches fits."""
    return any(notch_fits(a, notch) for notch in piece)


def assembles(puzzle: FramedPuzzle, a: Assembly) -> bool:
    """a assembles the puzzle iff every clause piece snaps into place."""
    return all(piece_snaps(a, piece) for piece in puzzle)


def assembly_space(puzzle: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> Set[Assembly]:
    """A(P): the complete set of assemblies, by enumeration of the cube."""
    return {a for a in cube(n) if assembles(puzzle, a)}


def comp_puzzle(puzzle: FramedPuzzle) -> FramedPuzzle:
    """Global tab-blank complementation: re-mill every notch for -p."""
    return [[(i, not p) for (i, p) in piece] for piece in puzzle]


def comp_assembly(a: Assembly) -> Assembly:
    """sigma: Boolean negation of an assembly (swap every variable piece)."""
    return tuple(not bit for bit in a)


def combined_space(puzzle: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> Set[Assembly]:
    """C(P) = A(P) u A(P*), the untagged combined assembly space."""
    return assembly_space(puzzle, n) | assembly_space(comp_puzzle(puzzle), n)


def polarity_gauge(space: Iterable[Assembly]) -> Set[Assembly]:
    """Gauge: the assemblies whose variable-0 piece exposes a tab (True)."""
    return {a for a in space if a[0]}


def orbits(space: Iterable[Assembly]) -> List[Tuple[Assembly, Assembly]]:
    """The free complementation orbits {a, sigma(a)}, one per gauge point."""
    return [(g, comp_assembly(g)) for g in sorted(polarity_gauge(space))]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Complete expressiveness: exclusion pieces
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exclusion_piece(b: Assembly) -> ClausePiece:
    """E_b: the single clause piece that forbids exactly the assembly b.

    Its notch for variable i is milled for the opposite of b[i], so it snaps
    into place under a iff a differs from b somewhere, i.e. iff a != b.
    """
    return [(i, not bit) for i, bit in enumerate(b)]


def puzzle_of_set(S: Set[Assembly], n: int) -> FramedPuzzle:
    """P_S: the framed puzzle whose assembly space is exactly S.

    One exclusion piece per point of the cube that must NOT assemble, so
    |P_S| = 2^n - |S|.
    """
    return [exclusion_piece(b) for b in cube(n) if b not in S]


def stable_set_of_size(n: int, two_k: int) -> Set[Assembly]:
    """A complement-stable subset of the cube of prescribed even size 2k.

    Take k gauge points and adjoin their complements.
    """
    assert two_k % 2 == 0 and two_k <= 2 ** n, "size must be even and <= 2^n"
    k = two_k // 2
    gauge = sorted(polarity_gauge(cube(n)))
    chosen = gauge[:k]
    return set(chosen) | {comp_assembly(g) for g in chosen}


def stable_spaces(n: int) -> List[FrozenSet[Assembly]]:
    """Enumerate all complement-stable subsets of the cube.

    By the gauge parameterisation these are exactly T u sigma(T) for
    T a subset of the 2^(n-1)-element gauge, so there are 2^(2^(n-1)) of them.
    """
    gauge = sorted(polarity_gauge(cube(n)))
    out: List[FrozenSet[Assembly]] = []
    for r in range(len(gauge) + 1):
        for T in itertools.combinations(gauge, r):
            out.append(frozenset(set(T) | {comp_assembly(g) for g in T}))
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Sign of complementation as a permutation of the cube
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def permutation_sign(perm: Dict[Assembly, Assembly]) -> int:
    """Sign of a permutation given as a dictionary, via cycle decomposition."""
    seen: Set[Assembly] = set()
    sign = 1
    for start in perm:
        if start in seen:
            continue
        length = 0
        x = start
        while x not in seen:
            seen.add(x)
            x = perm[x]
            length += 1
        if length % 2 == 0:          # a cycle of even length is an odd permutation
            sign = -sign
    return sign


def comp_sign(n: int) -> int:
    """sgn(sigma) computed by explicit cycle decomposition of the cube."""
    return permutation_sign({a: comp_assembly(a) for a in cube(n)})


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  The d-ary cyclic model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def dcube(n: int, d: int) -> List[DAssembly]:
    """All d^n depth assignments in (Z/d)^n."""
    return [tuple(v) for v in itertools.product(range(d), repeat=n)]


def d_assembles(puzzle: DFramedPuzzle, a: DAssembly) -> bool:
    """Each clause piece needs one notch whose milled depth matches its variable."""
    return all(any(a[i] == t for (i, t) in piece) for piece in puzzle)


def shift_puzzle(puzzle: DFramedPuzzle, t: int, d: int) -> DFramedPuzzle:
    """Deepen every mill by t."""
    return [[(i, (s + t) % d) for (i, s) in piece] for piece in puzzle]


def shift_assembly(a: DAssembly, t: int, d: int) -> DAssembly:
    """Deepen every variable piece by t."""
    return tuple((v + t) % d for v in a)


def d_combined(puzzle: DFramedPuzzle, n: int, d: int) -> Set[DAssembly]:
    """The union of the assembly spaces of all d depth shifts."""
    out: Set[DAssembly] = set()
    for t in range(d):
        shifted = shift_puzzle(puzzle, t, d)
        out |= {a for a in dcube(n, d) if d_assembles(shifted, a)}
    return out


def depth_gauge(space: Iterable[DAssembly]) -> Set[DAssembly]:
    """Depth gauge: assemblies whose variable-0 piece is milled to depth 0."""
    return {a for a in space if a[0] == 0}


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pretty-printing helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def fmt(a: Sequence[bool]) -> str:
    return "".join("1" if bit else "0" for bit in a)


def fmt_d(a: Sequence[int]) -> str:
    return "".join(str(v) for v in a)


def show_puzzle(puzzle: FramedPuzzle) -> str:
    if not puzzle:
        return "(no clause pieces)"
    return " AND ".join(
        "(" + " OR ".join(("" if p else "-") + f"x{i}" for (i, p) in piece) + ")"
        for piece in puzzle
    )


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_exact_transport() -> None:
    banner("1.  EXACT TRANSPORT:  A(P*) = sigma(A(P))")
    n = 3
    # P = (x0 or x1) and (-x1 or x2) and (x0 or -x2)
    P: FramedPuzzle = [[(0, True), (1, True)],
                       [(1, False), (2, True)],
                       [(0, True), (2, False)]]
    print(f"n = {n},   P  = {show_puzzle(P)}")
    print(f"          P* = {show_puzzle(comp_puzzle(P))}")

    A = assembly_space(P, n)
    Astar = assembly_space(comp_puzzle(P), n)
    sigmaA = {comp_assembly(a) for a in A}

    print(f"\n  A(P)          = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(A))}}}   |A(P)|  = {len(A)}")
    print(f"  A(P*)         = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(Astar))}}}   |A(P*)| = {len(Astar)}")
    print(f"  sigma(A(P))   = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(sigmaA))}}}")
    assert Astar == sigmaA, "exact transport failed"
    assert len(Astar) == len(A)
    print("\n  VERIFIED: A(P*) = sigma(A(P)) and the two spaces are equinumerous.")


def demo_parity_and_orbits() -> None:
    banner("2-3-5.  UNTAGGED PARITY, SELF-DUAL PARITY, AND ORBIT DECOMPOSITION")
    n = 3
    P: FramedPuzzle = [[(0, True), (1, True)],
                       [(1, False), (2, True)],
                       [(0, True), (2, False)]]
    C = combined_space(P, n)
    G = polarity_gauge(C)
    print(f"  C(P) = A(P) u A(P*) = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(C))}}}")
    print(f"  |C(P)| = {len(C)}   (even: {len(C) % 2 == 0})")
    print(f"  Gauge(C(P))  = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(G))}}}   |Gauge| = {len(G)}")
    print(f"  |C(P)| = 2 * |Gauge| :  {len(C)} = 2 * {len(G)}   -> {len(C) == 2 * len(G)}")
    print("  Free orbits:")
    for g, s in orbits(C):
        print(f"      {{ {fmt(g)} , {fmt(s)} }}")
    assert len(C) % 2 == 0 and len(C) == 2 * len(G)

    print("\n  --- A self-dual example -------------------------------------------")
    # P2 = (x0 or -x0):  tautological piece; assembly space = whole cube.
    P2: FramedPuzzle = [[(0, True), (0, False)]]
    A2 = assembly_space(P2, n)
    A2star = assembly_space(comp_puzzle(P2), n)
    print(f"  P2 = {show_puzzle(P2)}")
    print(f"  A(P2*) == A(P2) ?  {A2star == A2}    |A(P2)| = {len(A2)}  (even: {len(A2) % 2 == 0})")
    print("  Self-duality does NOT create a fixed point: it collapses the two")
    print("  spaces onto one, on which complementation still acts freely.")
    assert A2star == A2 and len(A2) % 2 == 0

    print("\n  --- Random stress test --------------------------------------------")
    rng = random.Random(20260824)
    failures = 0
    for trial in range(400):
        m = rng.randint(0, 5)
        nn = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Pr: FramedPuzzle = [
            [(rng.randrange(nn), rng.choice([True, False]))
             for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3))]
            for _ in range(m)
        ]
        Cr = combined_space(Pr, nn)
        if len(Cr) % 2 != 0 or len(Cr) != 2 * len(polarity_gauge(Cr)):
            failures += 1
    print(f"  400 random puzzles (n = 1..4):  parity + orbit identity failures = {failures}")
    assert failures == 0


def demo_sharpness_at_zero() -> None:
    banner("4.  SHARPNESS: THE BOUNDARY IS n = 0, NOT SELF-DUALITY")
    P0: FramedPuzzle = []
    A0 = assembly_space(P0, 0)
    C0 = combined_space(P0, 0)
    print(f"  n = 0.  The cube has {len(cube(0))} point: the empty assembly.")
    print(f"  Every zero-variable puzzle is self-complementary: P* == P ?  "
          f"{comp_puzzle(P0) == P0}")
    print(f"  A(P) = {A0},  |C(P)| = {len(C0)}   -> ODD, so parity genuinely fails.")
    print(f"  sigma fixes the empty assembly: {comp_assembly(()) == ()}")
    print("  This is the unique fixed configuration anywhere in the theory.")
    assert len(C0) == 1


def demo_sign() -> None:
    banner("6.  SIGN OF COMPLEMENTATION AS A PERMUTATION OF THE CUBE")
    print("   n | cube size | #transpositions 2^(n-1) | sgn(sigma) computed | predicted")
    print("  ---+-----------+-------------------------+---------------------+----------")
    for n in range(1, 8):
        computed = comp_sign(n)
        predicted = (-1) ** (2 ** (n - 1))
        assert computed == predicted
        print(f"   {n} | {2**n:9d} | {2**(n-1):23d} | {computed:19d} | {predicted:9d}")
    print("\n  Complementation is an ODD permutation exactly when n = 1;")
    print("  for every n >= 2 it is even.")


def demo_expressiveness() -> None:
    banner("7.  COMPLETE EXPRESSIVENESS: EVERY SUBSET IS AN ASSEMBLY SPACE")
    n = 3
    print(f"  n = {n}.  Round-tripping all {2**(2**n)} subsets of the cube:")
    total = 0
    for r in range(2 ** n + 1):
        for S_tuple in itertools.combinations(cube(n), r):
            S = set(S_tuple)
            P = puzzle_of_set(S, n)
            assert assembly_space(P, n) == S, "expressiveness failed"
            assert len(P) == 2 ** n - len(S), "piece count formula failed"
            total += 1
    print(f"  VERIFIED for all {total} subsets:  A(P_S) = S  and  |P_S| = 2^n - |S|.")

    print("\n  Example.  S = {110} (a singleton) on n = 3 variables:")
    S = {(True, True, False)}
    P = puzzle_of_set(S, 3)
    print(f"      pieces: {len(P)} = 2^3 - 1")
    print(f"      P_S  = {show_puzzle(P)}")
    print(f"      A(P_S) = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(assembly_space(P, 3)))}}}")
    C = combined_space(P, 3)
    print(f"      C(P_S) = {{{', '.join(fmt(a) for a in sorted(C))}}}   |C| = {len(C)} (even)")


def demo_spectrum() -> None:
    banner("8.  THE EXACT SPECTRUM OF COMBINED ASSEMBLY COUNTS")
    for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        achievable = set()
        # every even 2k <= 2^n is achieved, by realising a stable set of that size
        for two_k in range(0, 2 ** n + 1, 2):
            S = stable_set_of_size(n, two_k)
            P = puzzle_of_set(S, n)
            c = len(combined_space(P, n))
            assert c == two_k, f"synthesis failed: wanted {two_k}, got {c}"
            achievable.add(c)
        predicted = set(range(0, 2 ** n + 1, 2))
        assert achievable == predicted
        print(f"  n = {n}:  achievable combined counts = {sorted(achievable)}"
              f"   = all even m <= 2^{n} = {2**n}")

    print("\n  Single-puzzle counts are UNCONSTRAINED (odd counts occur):")
    n = 3
    singles = []
    for k in range(2 ** n + 1):
        S = set(cube(n)[:k])
        P = puzzle_of_set(S, n)
        singles.append(len(assembly_space(P, n)))
    print(f"  n = 3:  realised single counts = {singles}")
    assert singles == list(range(2 ** n + 1))
    print("  This is exactly why parity must be a statement about the")
    print("  complement-stable UNION, never about one assembly space.")


def demo_density() -> None:
    banner("9.  DENSITY OF SELF-DUALITY: A SQUARE-ROOT LAW")
    print("   n | stable spaces (enumerated) | 2^(2^(n-1)) | all spaces 2^(2^n) | square?")
    print("  ---+----------------------------+-------------+--------------------+--------")
    for n in (1, 2, 3):
        enumerated = len(set(stable_spaces(n)))
        predicted = 2 ** (2 ** (n - 1))
        total = 2 ** (2 ** n)
        assert enumerated == predicted
        assert predicted * predicted == total
        print(f"   {n} | {enumerated:26d} | {predicted:11d} | {total:18d} |"
              f"   {predicted * predicted == total}")
    print("\n  For n = 4 the formula gives 2^8 = 256 stable spaces out of 2^16 = 65536.")
    print("  Self-duality is exactly a square-root condition: doubly-exponentially")
    print("  rare, yet realised in EVERY admissible even size (see section 8).")

    print("\n  Every stable space really is a self-dual assembly space:")
    n = 3
    checked = 0
    for S in set(stable_spaces(n)):
        P = puzzle_of_set(set(S), n)
        assert assembly_space(comp_puzzle(P), n) == assembly_space(P, n) == set(S)
        checked += 1
    print(f"      verified for all {checked} complement-stable spaces on n = 3.")


def demo_cyclic() -> None:
    banner("10.  CYCLIC GENERALISATION: d INTERLOCK DEPTHS")
    n, d = 2, 3
    Q: DFramedPuzzle = [[(0, 1)], [(1, 2)]]
    print(f"  n = {n}, d = {d}.  Q has one piece milled for depth 1 at x0,")
    print(f"                   and one milled for depth 2 at x1.")
    for t in range(d):
        shifted = shift_puzzle(Q, t, d)
        space = {a for a in dcube(n, d) if d_assembles(shifted, a)}
        print(f"      shift {t}:  A_d(Q^+{t}) = "
              f"{{{', '.join(fmt_d(a) for a in sorted(space))}}}")
    C = d_combined(Q, n, d)
    G = depth_gauge(C)
    print(f"  Combined C_d(Q) = {{{', '.join(fmt_d(a) for a in sorted(C))}}}")
    print(f"  |C_d(Q)| = {len(C)},  depth gauge size = {len(G)},  "
          f"|C| = d * |gauge| : {len(C) == d * len(G)}")
    assert len(C) % d == 0 and len(C) == d * len(G)

    print("\n  Random stress test of the divisibility law:")
    rng = random.Random(7)
    print("   d | trials | all divisible by d | all equal d*|gauge|")
    print("  ---+--------+--------------------+--------------------")
    for d in (2, 3, 4, 5):
        ok_div = ok_gauge = 0
        trials = 120
        for _ in range(trials):
            nn = rng.randint(1, 3)
            R: DFramedPuzzle = [
                [(rng.randrange(nn), rng.randrange(d)) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 2))]
                for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 4))
            ]
            Cd = d_combined(R, nn, d)
            ok_div += (len(Cd) % d == 0)
            ok_gauge += (len(Cd) == d * len(depth_gauge(Cd)))
        assert ok_div == trials and ok_gauge == trials
        print(f"   {d} | {trials:6d} | {ok_div:18d} | {ok_gauge:19d}")
    print("\n  Tab-blank parity is the d = 2 slice: the constraint on solution")
    print("  counts is the ORDER of the group acting freely on configurations.")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__.split("Run:")[0].strip())
    demo_exact_transport()
    demo_parity_and_orbits()
    demo_sharpness_at_zero()
    demo_sign()
    demo_expressiveness()
    demo_spectrum()
    demo_density()
    demo_cyclic()
    banner("ALL DEMONSTRATIONS COMPLETED -- every assertion held.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Exhaustive Census of Framed Puzzles on Few Variables
demos.description: Where the main demonstration uses chosen and random examples, this one is exhaustive. For n = 1, 2, 3 it enumerates every framed puzzle built from a bounded catalogue of distinct clause pieces -- a clause piece being any subset of the 2n available notches -- amounting to tens of thousands of puzzles, and for every single one it verifies exact transport, equinumerosity, untagged parity, parity of the intersection, self-dual parity, and the orbit identity |C(P)| = 2|Gauge(C(P))|. It then tabulates which assembly spaces, which complement-stable spaces, which single counts and which combined counts are realised inside the budget, and compares them with the predicted 2^(2^n) subsets, 2^(2^(n-1)) stable spaces and the even-numbers spectrum. No sampling is used anywhere: the enumeration is complete for the stated range, so a single counterexample would surface.
demos.code:
"""Exhaustive Census of Framed Puzzles on Few Variables.

Where the main demonstration checks the theorems on chosen and random examples,
this one is EXHAUSTIVE.  For n = 1, 2, 3 it enumerates every framed puzzle built
from the full catalogue of distinct clause pieces (a clause piece is a subset of
the 2n possible notches, so there are 2^(2n) of them, and a puzzle is any subset
of that catalogue -- repetition and order are irrelevant to the assembly space).

For every single puzzle it verifies, with no sampling:

  * Exact Transport         A(P*) = sigma(A(P)),  |A(P*)| = |A(P)|;
  * Untagged Parity         |A(P) u A(P*)| is even;
  * Intersection Parity     |A(P) n A(P*)| is even;
  * Self-Dual Parity        A(P*) = A(P)  =>  |A(P)| is even;
  * Orbit Identity          |C(P)| = 2 |Gauge(C(P))|.

It then tabulates the realised spectra and the census of assembly spaces,
confirming that assembly spaces exhaust the 2^(2^n) subsets of the cube and
that the complement-stable ones number exactly 2^(2^(n-1)).

Run:  python3 demo2_census.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, List, Set, Tuple

Assembly = Tuple[bool, ...]
Notch = Tuple[int, bool]
ClausePiece = Tuple[Notch, ...]
FramedPuzzle = Tuple[ClausePiece, ...]


def cube(n: int) -> List[Assembly]:
    return [tuple(bits) for bits in itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n)]


def all_pieces(n: int) -> List[ClausePiece]:
    """Every clause piece on n variables: a subset of the 2n available notches."""
    notches: List[Notch] = [(i, p) for i in range(n) for p in (True, False)]
    out: List[ClausePiece] = []
    for r in range(len(notches) + 1):
        out.extend(itertools.combinations(notches, r))
    return out


def assembly_space(P: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> FrozenSet[Assembly]:
    return frozenset(a for a in cube(n)
                     if all(any(a[i] == p for (i, p) in c) for c in P))


def comp_puzzle(P: FramedPuzzle) -> FramedPuzzle:
    return tuple(tuple((i, not p) for (i, p) in c) for c in P)


def comp_assembly(a: Assembly) -> Assembly:
    return tuple(not b for b in a)


def gauge(S: FrozenSet[Assembly]) -> Set[Assembly]:
    return {a for a in S if a[0]}


def census(n: int, max_pieces: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Exhaustive verification over all puzzles with at most `max_pieces` pieces."""
    catalogue = all_pieces(n)
    spaces: Set[FrozenSet[Assembly]] = set()
    stable: Set[FrozenSet[Assembly]] = set()
    single_counts: Set[int] = set()
    combined_counts: Set[int] = set()
    checked = 0

    for r in range(max_pieces + 1):
        for P in itertools.combinations(catalogue, r):
            A = assembly_space(P, n)
            A_star = assembly_space(comp_puzzle(P), n)
            sigma_A = frozenset(comp_assembly(a) for a in A)

            assert A_star == sigma_A, "exact transport failed"
            assert len(A_star) == len(A), "equinumerosity failed"

            C = A | A_star
            assert len(C) % 2 == 0, "untagged parity failed"
            assert len(A & A_star) % 2 == 0, "intersection parity failed"
            assert len(C) == 2 * len(gauge(frozenset(C))), "orbit identity failed"
            if A_star == A:
                assert len(A) % 2 == 0, "self-dual parity failed"
                stable.add(A)

            spaces.add(A)
            single_counts.add(len(A))
            combined_counts.add(len(C))
            checked += 1

    return {
        "n": n,
        "puzzles_checked": checked,
        "distinct_spaces": len(spaces),
        "spaces_predicted": 2 ** (2 ** n),
        "stable_spaces": len(stable),
        "stable_predicted": 2 ** (2 ** (n - 1)),
        "single_counts": sorted(single_counts),
        "combined_counts": sorted(combined_counts),
        "combined_predicted": list(range(0, 2 ** n + 1, 2)),
    }


def main() -> None:
    print("Exhaustive census of framed puzzles")
    print("=" * 74)
    # The budget bounds the number of DISTINCT clause pieces.  Small budgets do
    # not realise every assembly space -- complete expressiveness needs up to
    # 2^n exclusion pieces -- but every puzzle inside the budget is checked.
    for n, max_pieces in ((1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 3)):
        report = census(n, max_pieces)
        print(f"\nn = {n}   (all puzzles with at most {max_pieces} distinct clause pieces)")
        print(f"  puzzles verified            : {report['puzzles_checked']}")
        print(f"  every theorem held          : yes (assertions passed)")
        print(f"  spaces seen in this budget  : {report['distinct_spaces']}"
              f"   of the {report['spaces_predicted']} subsets of the cube")
        print(f"  stable spaces in this budget: {report['stable_spaces']}"
              f"   of the {report['stable_predicted']} that exist"
              f"   (formula 2^(2^(n-1)))")
        print(f"  realised single counts      : {report['single_counts']}")
        print(f"  realised combined counts    : {report['combined_counts']}")
        print(f"  full combined spectrum      : {report['combined_predicted']}"
              f"   (the rest need more pieces)")

    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print("Every puzzle examined satisfied exact transport, untagged parity,")
    print("intersection parity, self-dual parity and the orbit identity.")
    print("No sampling was used: the enumeration is complete for the stated range.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Exhaustive Assembly-Space Enumeration with Complementation Transport
algorithms.description: The base computation of the entire theory. Given a framed puzzle P on n variables with m clause pieces and L notches in total, it enumerates the 2^n points of the Boolean cube and tests each against every clause piece, producing the complete assembly space A(P); it repeats the computation for the complemented puzzle P*, and returns a certificate bundling the two spaces, the transport identity A(P*) = sigma(A(P)), the equinumerosity |A(P*)| = |A(P)|, and the parity of both the union and the intersection. The cost is O(2^n L) time and O(2^n) space, and this is essentially optimal for exact enumeration: deciding whether A(P) is nonempty is NP-complete and counting |A(P)| is #P-hard, so no algorithm polynomial in the description length of P is expected. In the pipeline this routine is the oracle against which every structural theorem is empirically checked.
algorithms.code:
"""Exhaustive Assembly-Space Enumeration with Complementation Transport.

Computes A(P), A(P*) and the untagged combined space C(P) = A(P) u A(P*),
and certifies the Exact Transport Theorem  A(P*) = sigma(A(P))  and the
Parity Theorem  2 | |C(P)|  (valid for n >= 1).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple

Assembly = Tuple[bool, ...]
Notch = Tuple[int, bool]
ClausePiece = List[Notch]
FramedPuzzle = List[ClausePiece]


def cube(n: int) -> List[Assembly]:
    """The 2^n points of the Boolean cube, lexicographically ordered."""
    return [tuple(bits) for bits in itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n)]


def assembles(puzzle: FramedPuzzle, a: Assembly) -> bool:
    """Every clause piece must have at least one notch (i, p) with a[i] == p."""
    return all(any(a[i] == p for (i, p) in piece) for piece in puzzle)


def assembly_space(puzzle: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> Set[Assembly]:
    """A(P), by enumeration of the cube.  Cost O(2^n * L), L = total notches."""
    return {a for a in cube(n) if assembles(puzzle, a)}


def comp_puzzle(puzzle: FramedPuzzle) -> FramedPuzzle:
    """Global tab-blank complementation: re-mill every notch for -p."""
    return [[(i, not p) for (i, p) in piece] for piece in puzzle]


def comp_assembly(a: Assembly) -> Assembly:
    """sigma: Boolean negation of an assembly."""
    return tuple(not b for b in a)


def transport_report(puzzle: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Full certificate of transport, equinumerosity and parity."""
    A = assembly_space(puzzle, n)
    A_star = assembly_space(comp_puzzle(puzzle), n)
    sigma_A = {comp_assembly(a) for a in A}
    C = A | A_star
    return {
        "n": n,
        "A": sorted(A),
        "A_star": sorted(A_star),
        "transport_holds": A_star == sigma_A,
        "equinumerous": len(A) == len(A_star),
        "combined_count": len(C),
        "combined_even": len(C) % 2 == 0,
        "intersection_count": len(A & A_star),
        "intersection_even": len(A & A_star) % 2 == 0,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    P: FramedPuzzle = [[(0, True), (1, True)], [(1, False), (2, True)]]
    for key, value in transport_report(P, 3).items():
        print(f"{key:20s} : {value}")

algorithms.name: Polarity-Gauge Orbit Decomposition and Parity Certificate
algorithms.description: Upgrades the parity conclusion from an existence statement to an explicit pairing. The polarity gauge of a set S of assemblies is the subset whose first variable piece exposes a tab; because complementation flips exactly that coordinate, the gauge meets each free orbit precisely once, and is therefore a computable section of the orbit map. The algorithm first verifies that S is complement-stable, then returns the gauge, the list of orbits {g, sigma(g)}, a proof-carrying check that these orbits partition S without overlap or omission, and the identity |S| = 2|Gauge(S)| from which evenness follows immediately. Its cost is a single linear pass, O(|S|) time, which is asymptotically cheaper than the enumeration that produced S and makes the decomposition essentially free once the space is known. Structurally this is the algorithm that reveals parity to be the shadow of a decomposition: the gauge cardinality IS the number of orbits, so the same routine simultaneously certifies evenness and counts the symmetry classes.

algorithms.name: Exclusion-Piece Realisation of a Prescribed Assembly Space
algorithms.description: The constructive core of the expressiveness half of the theory. The exclusion piece E_b carries exactly one notch per variable, milled for the opposite of b's choice at that variable; consequently it snaps into place under an assembly a if and only if a differs from b in at least one coordinate, that is, if and only if a is not b. A single clause piece therefore forbids exactly one point of the configuration space and permits all others. Listing one such piece for each point that must not assemble realises an arbitrary prescribed subset S as the exact assembly space, using 2^n - |S| pieces and O((2^n - |S|) n) notches in total, all constructed in a single pass over the cube. The realisation is maximally redundant by design -- it is a certificate of surjectivity, not a minimisation -- and it is what converts the parity constraint into a sharp characterisation: since every subset occurs, no counting law beyond the ones forced by the free involution can hold.

algorithms.name: Even-Count Synthesis by Gauge Doubling
algorithms.description: Realises the sufficiency half of the Combined Spectrum Theorem. Given a target even number 2k not exceeding 2^n, the algorithm selects k points from the polarity gauge of the full cube -- there are 2^(n-1) of them, so the selection is always possible -- and adjoins their complements. The resulting set S is complement-stable by construction and has exactly 2k elements, the two halves being disjoint because gauge points carry a tab at variable 0 and their complements a blank. Realising S with exclusion pieces then yields a puzzle whose mirror has the same assembly space, so the untagged combined space is S itself and its cardinality is exactly the target. The construction runs in O(2^n n) time. Paired with the Parity Theorem, which forbids odd targets, it pins the achievable combined counts to precisely the even numbers up to 2^n -- the exact point at which the constraint side and the expressiveness side of the theory meet. The same output doubles as a witness that self-dual assembly spaces exist in every admissible even size.

algorithms.name: Cyclic Depth-Shift Divisibility Certificate
algorithms.description: Generalises the whole parity mechanism from two interlock shapes to d milling depths. A variable piece now exposes an element of Z/d, a notch is milled for a required depth, and deepening every mill by t is an order-d symmetry that transports assembly spaces exactly: shifting the puzzle and the assembly by the same amount preserves assembly. The algorithm forms the pooled combined space of all d depth shifts, which is shift-stable, computes the depth gauge consisting of those assemblies whose variable 0 sits at depth 0, and certifies the bijection (g, t) -> g + t from gauge x Z/d onto the pooled space. From that bijection the identity |C| = d x |gauge| follows, and divisibility of the pooled count by d is immediate. The cost is O(d^(n+1) L) since each of the d shifted puzzles is tested against all d^n depth assignments. Setting d = 2 recovers the tab-blank parity theorem, exhibiting parity as one slice of a divisibility law whose modulus is the order of the group acting freely on the configuration space.
algorithms.code:
"""Cyclic Depth-Shift Divisibility Certificate.

Replace tab/blank by d interlock depths: a variable piece exposes an element
of Z/d and a notch is milled for a required depth.  "Deepen every mill by t"
is an order-d symmetry.  For n >= 1 the combined space over all d shifts,

    C_d(P) = union over t in Z/d of A_d(P^{+t}),

is shift-stable and the map (g, t) |-> g + t is a bijection
    DepthGauge(C_d(P)) x Z/d  ->  C_d(P),
so |C_d(P)| = d * |DepthGauge| and in particular d divides |C_d(P)|.
Tab-blank parity is the d = 2 slice.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple

DAssembly = Tuple[int, ...]
DNotch = Tuple[int, int]
DPuzzle = List[List[DNotch]]


def dcube(n: int, d: int) -> List[DAssembly]:
    """The d^n depth assignments in (Z/d)^n."""
    return [tuple(v) for v in itertools.product(range(d), repeat=n)]


def d_assembles(P: DPuzzle, a: DAssembly) -> bool:
    return all(any(a[i] == t for (i, t) in piece) for piece in P)


def shift_puzzle(P: DPuzzle, t: int, d: int) -> DPuzzle:
    """Deepen every mill by t."""
    return [[(i, (s + t) % d) for (i, s) in piece] for piece in P]


def d_combined(P: DPuzzle, n: int, d: int) -> Set[DAssembly]:
    """Union of the assembly spaces of all d depth shifts.  Cost O(d^(n+1) L)."""
    out: Set[DAssembly] = set()
    for t in range(d):
        Pt = shift_puzzle(P, t, d)
        out |= {a for a in dcube(n, d) if d_assembles(Pt, a)}
    return out


def depth_gauge(S: Set[DAssembly]) -> Set[DAssembly]:
    """Section of the shift-orbit map: variable 0 milled to depth 0."""
    return {a for a in S if a[0] == 0}


def divisibility_certificate(P: DPuzzle, n: int, d: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Combined count, gauge size, and the verified identity |C| = d |gauge|."""
    C = d_combined(P, n, d)
    G = depth_gauge(C)
    return {
        "d": d,
        "n": n,
        "combined_count": len(C),
        "gauge_size": len(G),
        "identity_holds": len(C) == d * len(G),
        "divisible_by_d": len(C) % d == 0,
        "orbits": [tuple(tuple((v + t) % d for v in g) for t in range(d))
                   for g in sorted(G)],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    Q: DPuzzle = [[(0, 1)], [(1, 2)]]
    cert = divisibility_certificate(Q, n=2, d=3)
    for key in ("d", "n", "combined_count", "gauge_size",
                "identity_holds", "divisible_by_d"):
        print(f"{key:18s} : {cert[key]}")
    for orbit in cert["orbits"]:          # type: ignore[index]
        print("   shift orbit:", " -> ".join("".join(map(str, a)) for a in orbit))

visualizations.name: Complementation as a Perfect Matching on the Boolean Cube
visualizations.description: Draws the 2^n assemblies of the Boolean cube as a ring of labelled nodes, arranged so that every assembly sits diametrically opposite its complement, and overlays the perfect matching induced by complementation. Nodes are coloured by membership: assemblies of the puzzle, of its mirror, of both, or of neither; the chords lying inside the combined space are highlighted. The picture makes the parity theorem immediate -- each highlighted chord is a free two-element orbit, so the combined space is a disjoint union of pairs and cannot have odd size. A companion panel shows the single degenerate case, n = 0, where the cube is one point fixed by complementation, the combined count is one, and parity genuinely fails: the unique fixed configuration in the whole theory.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the complementation matching on the Boolean cube.

Draws the 2^n assemblies of the Boolean cube as a ring of labelled nodes and
overlays the perfect matching induced by complementation, sigma(a) = -a.
Nodes are coloured by membership: assemblies of P, of its complement P*, of
both, or of neither.  Every chord of the matching joins a node of A(P) to a
node of A(P*), which is precisely why the combined space is even: the chords
restricted to C(P) partition it into two-element orbits.

A second panel plots the same matching for the degenerate case n = 0, where
the cube is a single point fixed by complementation -- the unique fixed
configuration in the theory, and the unique failure of parity.

Run:  python3 viz1_orbits.py      (writes complementation_orbits.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
from typing import List, Set, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Assembly = Tuple[bool, ...]
FramedPuzzle = List[List[Tuple[int, bool]]]


def cube(n: int) -> List[Assembly]:
    return [tuple(bits) for bits in itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n)]


def assembles(P: FramedPuzzle, a: Assembly) -> bool:
    return all(any(a[i] == p for (i, p) in piece) for piece in P)


def assembly_space(P: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> Set[Assembly]:
    return {a for a in cube(n) if assembles(P, a)}


def comp_puzzle(P: FramedPuzzle) -> FramedPuzzle:
    return [[(i, not p) for (i, p) in piece] for piece in P]


def comp_assembly(a: Assembly) -> Assembly:
    return tuple(not b for b in a)


def label(a: Assembly) -> str:
    return "".join("1" if b else "0" for b in a) or "\u03b5"


def main() -> None:
    n = 4
    # P = (x0 or x1) and (-x1 or x2) and (x0 or -x3)
    P: FramedPuzzle = [[(0, True), (1, True)],
                       [(1, False), (2, True)],
                       [(0, True), (3, False)]]

    A = assembly_space(P, n)
    A_star = assembly_space(comp_puzzle(P), n)
    C = A | A_star
    points = cube(n)
    # place a and sigma(a) diametrically opposite so chords are diameters
    gauge = sorted(a for a in points if a[0])
    order = gauge + [comp_assembly(g) for g in gauge]
    pos = {}
    m = len(order)
    for idx, a in enumerate(order):
        theta = 2 * math.pi * idx / m + math.pi / 2
        pos[a] = (math.cos(theta), math.sin(theta))

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7.5),
                             gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2.3, 1]})
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")

    drawn = set()
    for a in order:
        b = comp_assembly(a)
        if (b, a) in drawn:
            continue
        drawn.add((a, b))
        xa, ya = pos[a]
        xb, yb = pos[b]
        in_combined = a in C and b in C
        ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb],
                color="#c0392b" if in_combined else "#d8d8d8",
                lw=2.4 if in_combined else 0.9,
                zorder=1, alpha=0.95 if in_combined else 0.6)

    for a in order:
        x, y = pos[a]
        both = a in A and a in A_star
        if both:
            color, edge = "#8e44ad", "#4a235a"
        elif a in A:
            color, edge = "#2980b9", "#154360"
        elif a in A_star:
            color, edge = "#27ae60", "#145a32"
        else:
            color, edge = "#f2f2f2", "#9a9a9a"
        ax.scatter([x], [y], s=520, c=color, edgecolors=edge,
                   linewidths=1.6, zorder=3)
        ax.text(x, y, label(a), ha="center", va="center", zorder=4,
                fontsize=9, fontweight="bold",
                color="white" if a in C else "#555555")
        ax.text(1.16 * x, 1.16 * y, "", ha="center", va="center")

    ax.set_title(
        "Complementation as a perfect matching on the Boolean cube  (n = 4)\n"
        f"|A(P)| = {len(A)},  |A(P*)| = {len(A_star)},  "
        f"|C(P)| = {len(C)}  (even)  =  2 x {len(C)//2} free orbits",
        fontsize=13, pad=18)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.35, 1.35)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.35)

    handles = [
        plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=13, mfc="#2980b9",
                   mec="#154360", label="assembles $P$ only"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=13, mfc="#27ae60",
                   mec="#145a32", label="assembles $P^{*}$ only"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=13, mfc="#8e44ad",
                   mec="#4a235a", label="assembles both"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=13, mfc="#f2f2f2",
                   mec="#9a9a9a", label="assembles neither"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], color="#c0392b", lw=2.6,
                   label="free orbit inside $C(P)$"),
    ]
    ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", ncol=3,
              bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.09), frameon=False, fontsize=10)

    # Right panel: the degenerate case n = 0.
    ax2 = axes[1]
    ax2.set_aspect("equal")
    ax2.axis("off")
    ax2.scatter([0], [0], s=1400, c="#e67e22", edgecolors="#7e3f00", lw=2)
    ax2.text(0, 0, "\u03b5", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22,
             color="white", fontweight="bold")
    circle = plt.Circle((0.0, 0.28), 0.26, fill=False, color="#c0392b",
                        lw=2.4, zorder=2)
    ax2.add_patch(circle)
    ax2.set_xlim(-1, 1)
    ax2.set_ylim(-1, 1)
    ax2.set_title(
        "The one exception: n = 0\n"
        "the empty assembly is FIXED by complementation,\n"
        "the combined count is 1, and parity fails",
        fontsize=12, pad=18)

    fig.suptitle(
        "Freeness lives in the configuration space, not in the puzzle",
        fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", y=0.99)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.95))
    fig.savefig("complementation_orbits.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote complementation_orbits.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Exact Combined Spectrum and the Square-Root Census of Self-Duality
visualizations.description: Two panels that together display the sharp boundary of the theory. Panel A marks, for n = 1 through 5 and every candidate count m from 0 to 2^n, whether m is achievable as a combined assembly count. Achievable values are not assumed but explicitly synthesised by gauge doubling followed by exclusion-piece realisation, and the resulting pattern is exactly the even numbers: freeness forbids the odd ones, complete expressiveness supplies all the rest. Panel B plots the census of assembly spaces on a doubly logarithmic vertical scale, comparing the 2^(2^n) assembly spaces with the 2^(2^(n-1)) complement-stable ones. The two curves are parallel lines separated by an exact factor of two in the exponent-of-the-exponent, which is the visual signature of the square-root law: the number of self-dual assembly spaces squared is the total number of assembly spaces.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the exact spectrum of combined counts and the square-root law.

Panel A. For n = 1..5 it marks, for every m in {0,...,2^n}, whether m is the
combined assembly count of some framed puzzle on n variables.  The achievable
values are computed by explicit synthesis (gauge doubling + exclusion pieces),
never assumed; the result is exactly the even numbers <= 2^n -- freeness forces
evenness, complete expressiveness forces nothing else.

Panel B. The census of complement-stable assembly spaces.  There are
2^(2^(n-1)) of them against 2^(2^n) assembly spaces in total, so self-duality
is exactly a square-root condition.  The plot uses a doubly-logarithmic
vertical scale (log2 of log2 of the count) to make the exact halving visible.

Run:  python3 viz2_spectrum.py      (writes spectrum_and_census.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import List, Set, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Assembly = Tuple[bool, ...]
FramedPuzzle = List[List[Tuple[int, bool]]]


def cube(n: int) -> List[Assembly]:
    return [tuple(bits) for bits in itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n)]


def comp_assembly(a: Assembly) -> Assembly:
    return tuple(not b for b in a)


def synthesise(n: int, two_k: int) -> FramedPuzzle:
    """Gauge doubling + exclusion pieces: a puzzle with combined count 2k."""
    gauge = [a for a in cube(n) if a[0]]
    chosen = gauge[: two_k // 2]
    S: Set[Assembly] = set(chosen) | {comp_assembly(g) for g in chosen}
    return [[(i, not b) for i, b in enumerate(x)] for x in cube(n) if x not in S]


def combined_count(P: FramedPuzzle, n: int) -> int:
    def sp(Q: FramedPuzzle) -> Set[Assembly]:
        return {a for a in cube(n)
                if all(any(a[i] == p for (i, p) in c) for c in Q)}
    Pc = [[(i, not p) for (i, p) in c] for c in P]
    return len(sp(P) | sp(Pc))


def main() -> None:
    ns = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    fig, (axA, axB) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6.4))

    # ---- Panel A: achievable combined counts -------------------------------
    for row, n in enumerate(ns):
        achievable = set()
        for m in range(0, 2 ** n + 1, 2):
            assert combined_count(synthesise(n, m), n) == m
            achievable.add(m)
        for m in range(2 ** n + 1):
            hit = m in achievable
            axA.scatter([m], [row],
                        s=170 if hit else 90,
                        marker="s" if hit else "x",
                        c="#1f6f8b" if hit else "#cf6a6a",
                        linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
        axA.plot([0, 2 ** n], [row, row], color="#d5dde0", lw=1.2, zorder=1)

    axA.set_yticks(range(len(ns)))
    axA.set_yticklabels([f"$n = {n}$" for n in ns], fontsize=11)
    axA.set_xlabel("combined assembly count  $m = |C(P)|$", fontsize=11)
    axA.set_title("A.  The exact combined spectrum\n"
                  "squares: realised by an explicit puzzle;   "
                  "crosses: provably impossible",
                  fontsize=12.5)
    axA.set_xlim(-1, 2 ** ns[-1] + 1)
    axA.set_ylim(-0.7, len(ns) - 0.3)
    axA.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
    axA.text(0.98, 0.06,
             "achievable  $\\Leftrightarrow$  $m$ even and $m \\leq 2^{n}$",
             transform=axA.transAxes, fontsize=12, ha="right",
             color="#1f6f8b", fontweight="bold",
             bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc="#eaf3f6", ec="#1f6f8b"))

    # ---- Panel B: the square-root census ----------------------------------
    ms = list(range(1, 7))
    stable_exp = [2 ** (n - 1) for n in ms]      # log2 of the stable count
    total_exp = [2 ** n for n in ms]             # log2 of the total count
    axB.plot(ms, total_exp, "o-", color="#8e44ad", lw=2.4, ms=9,
             label="all assembly spaces:  $\\log_2 = 2^{n}$")
    axB.plot(ms, stable_exp, "s-", color="#e67e22", lw=2.4, ms=9,
             label="complement-stable spaces:  $\\log_2 = 2^{n-1}$")
    for n, s, t in zip(ms, stable_exp, total_exp):
        axB.annotate(f"$2^{{{s}}}$", (n, s), textcoords="offset points",
                     xytext=(6, -14), fontsize=9, color="#a55a06")
        axB.annotate(f"$2^{{{t}}}$", (n, t), textcoords="offset points",
                     xytext=(6, 6), fontsize=9, color="#5b2c6f")
    axB.set_yscale("log", base=2)
    axB.set_xlabel("number of variables  $n$", fontsize=11)
    axB.set_ylabel("$\\log_2$ of the number of spaces", fontsize=11)
    axB.set_title("B.  Self-duality is exactly a square-root condition\n"
                  "$(2^{2^{n-1}})^{2} = 2^{2^{n}}$",
                  fontsize=12.5)
    axB.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axB.legend(fontsize=10.5, loc="upper left", frameon=False)

    fig.suptitle("Constraint meets expressiveness: parity is the only law, "
                 "and self-duality is its square root",
                 fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93))
    fig.savefig("spectrum_and_census.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote spectrum_and_census.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Complementation Workbench: mill a puzzle, flip every notch, watch the solution space travel
interactive_demos.description: A hands-on laboratory for the central theorem. You build a framed puzzle notch by notch: each row is a clause piece and each cell can carry a tab notch, a blank notch, or nothing, for up to four variables. The widget then computes, live, the complete assembly space of the puzzle and of its global tab-blank complement, and renders the Boolean cube as a ring of nodes arranged so that every assembly sits opposite its complement -- making the chords of the complementation matching literal diameters. Nodes are coloured by whether they assemble the puzzle, the mirror, both or neither, and the orbits lying inside the combined space are highlighted. A live panel reports the four numbers that matter -- the two space sizes, the untagged combined count, and the polarity gauge -- and states, in words, exactly which theorem each of them witnesses: exact transport when the two sizes agree, parity when the combined count is twice the gauge, and the self-dual case when the two spaces coincide yet the count remains even. Preset buttons load a two-clause puzzle with a single free orbit and a genuinely self-dual example, and a randomiser lets you hunt, unsuccessfully, for an odd combined count.
interactive_demos.html:
The Complementation Workbench

Build a framed puzzle by milling notches. Each row is a clause piece; for every variable it can carry a tab notch (accepts the true piece), a blank notch (accepts the false piece), or nothing. A piece snaps into place as soon as one of its notches finds its mate; the puzzle assembles when every piece is happy. Now flip every notch at once — that is global tab–blank complementation — and watch the entire solution space travel to the mirror puzzle, paired off into two‑element orbits that never close on themselves.

1 · Mill the puzzle

2 · The Boolean cube and its matching

assembles P only assembles P* only assembles both neither free orbit in C(P)

3 · What the theorems say about this puzzle

|A(P)| — assemblies of P
0
|A(P*)| — assemblies of the mirror
0
|C(P)| = |A(P) ∪ A(P*)|
0
polarity gauge = number of free orbits

interactive_demos.title: Beyond Tab and Blank: the Depth-Shift Divisibility Explorer
interactive_demos.description: An interactive demonstration that parity was never about the number two. Here the two interlock shapes are replaced by d milling depths, so a variable piece exposes an element of Z/d and a notch is milled for a required depth; deepening every mill by one step becomes an order-d symmetry. You choose d between two and five and up to three variables, mill the clause pieces by cycling each cell through the available depths, and the widget displays all d depth-shifted puzzles side by side with their individual assembly spaces colour-coded by shift. Below them it pools the spaces into the combined space, computes the depth gauge -- those assemblies whose first variable sits at depth zero -- and reports the certificate that the pooled count equals d times the gauge, together with the resulting divisibility. Each orbit is printed as an explicit cycle of length d. Setting d = 2 collapses the display back to the tab-blank parity theorem, making visible that the modulus constraining solution counts is simply the order of the group acting freely on the configuration space.
interactive_demos.html:
Beyond Tab and Blank: the Depth-Shift Divisibility Explorer

Tab and blank are just two interlock shapes. Mill the pieces with d distinct depths instead: a variable piece now exposes a depth in $\{0,1,\dots,d-1\}$, a notch is milled for a required depth, and “deepen every mill by one step” becomes an order‑$d$ symmetry. Everything transports, and the parity law becomes a divisibility law: the assemblies of all $d$ depth‑shifted puzzles, pooled together, always number a multiple of $d$. Tab–blank parity is the d = 2 slice of this.

# Complementation as a Free Involution ### A guided tour: how flipping every tab and blank forces the number of solutions to be even — and why that is the *only* thing it forces --- ## 0. The party trick, and the theorem hiding behind it Take a jigsaw puzzle and do something perverse: on every piece, at every edge, turn every **tab** into a **blank** and every blank into a tab. Nothing else changes. Does the puzzle still go together? Of course. If two edges used to mate — tab into blank — they still mate, blank into tab. "Fits" was never about *which* shape you had; it was about the two shapes being *opposite*. That much is folklore. What this page is about is the theorem hiding underneath it: > The flip does not merely preserve solvability. It is a perfect, invertible transport of the **entire space of solutions**, and because it never fixes anything, it forces the total number of configurations solving the puzzle *or* its mirror to be **even** — always, with no exceptions beyond one degenerate case. And that single bit of parity is *all* it forces. By the end of this page you will have built such puzzles yourself, watched their solution spaces pair off, and seen exactly where the boundary between "constrained" and "free" is drawn.
Prerequisites — click if you'd like a refresher on the two ideas we lean on **An involution** is a map $\sigma$ with $\sigma(\sigma(x)) = x$: doing it twice returns you to where you began. Complementing every tab and blank is one. So is negating every bit of a bit-string. **A free action** is one with no fixed points: $\sigma(x) \neq x$ for every $x$. A free involution on a finite set chops it cleanly into two-element orbits $\{x, \sigma(x)\}$, which is why the set must have even size. This is the oldest parity argument there is, and it is the entire engine of what follows. (See [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action) and [involution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Involution_(mathematics)) for background.) The one subtlety: "free" is a property of the map *and the set it acts on*. Much of the story below is about noticing which set that actually is.
--- ## 1. Puzzles that compute To make the flip do real work, our puzzles need to be doing more than depicting a landscape. Fix $n$ **variables**. For each variable $i$ the box contains a matched pair of **variable pieces** — a *true* piece and a *false* piece — and the frame has exactly one socket for variable $i$, so you must commit to one of the two. A complete commitment is a point of the **Boolean cube** $$a \in \{\texttt{true},\texttt{false}\}^n,$$ and there are $2^n$ of them. The rest of the box holds **clause pieces**. A clause piece carries some **notches**, each milled for a specific variable $i$ and a required polarity $p$. That notch accepts the installed variable-$i$ piece exactly when the installed piece has polarity $p$. A clause piece is happy — it snaps into the frame — as soon as **at least one** of its notches finds its mate. So a commitment $a$ **assembles** the puzzle $P$ when every clause piece is happy, and the **assembly space** $A(P)$ is the set of all such $a$. > **Local dictionary.** The notch $(i,p)$ interlocks under $a$ if and only if $a_i = p$.
Where this dictionary comes from (and why it is exactly a lemma, not a definition) The physical statement is that the installed piece's output edge must *mate* with the notch's input edge. Encode a truth value as an edge shape by an injective map $\mathrm{enc}$, and mill the notch $(i,p)$ with the complement $\mathrm{enc}(p)^{\mathrm c}$. Mating means $$\mathrm{enc}(a_i) = \mathrm{enc}(p),$$ and since $\mathrm{enc}$ and edge complementation are both injective this is equivalent to $a_i = p$. Two injectivity facts, one biconditional; everything downstream is combinatorics.
If you know propositional logic, you have already noticed the shape of this: a notch is a literal, a clause piece is a disjunction, a puzzle is a conjunction of clauses, and an assembly is a satisfying assignment. That is deliberate. The physical language of tabs and blanks is a faithful presentation of [Boolean constraint satisfaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunctive_normal_form) in which our symmetry is an operation on the *hardware*, not on a syntax. --- ## 2. Build one and watch it flip Time to stop reading and start milling. In the workbench below, each row is a clause piece; click a cell to give it a tab notch, a blank notch, or nothing at all. The ring on the right is the Boolean cube, with every point coloured by what it assembles, and every **red chord** a pair $\{a, \lnot a\}$. Three things to try, in order: 1. Build $(x_0) \wedge (x_1)$ with the example button. One assembly for the puzzle, one for the mirror, combined count $2$: a single orbit. 2. Hit **randomise** a dozen times and watch the combined count. It is never odd. 3. Hit the **self-dual** example. Now the two spaces coincide — and the count is *still* even. Keep this in mind; it is the point where the original conjecture went wrong. {{interactive_demo:0}} Notice how the chords are laid out: every one is a **diameter** of the ring. That is not decoration. Points are placed so that $a$ sits opposite $\lnot a$, which makes the central claim visually obvious: no point can ever be its own opposite. --- ## 3. Transport, not preservation Here is the first theorem, and it is genuinely stronger than the party trick. > **Exact Transport Theorem.** For every framed puzzle $P$ and every commitment $a$, > $$\sigma(a) \text{ assembles } P^{*} \iff a \text{ assembles } P,$$ > where $\sigma(a)_i = \lnot a_i$ and $P^{*}$ is $P$ with every notch re-milled for the opposite polarity. Consequently > $$A(P^{*}) = \sigma\bigl(A(P)\bigr), \qquad |A(P^{*})| = |A(P)|.$$
Proof sketch — a two-line cascade from a one-line dictionary *Notch level.* The notch $(i,\lnot p)$ fits under $\sigma(a)$ iff $\lnot a_i = \lnot p$ iff $a_i = p$ iff $(i,p)$ fits under $a$. *Piece level.* Complementation matches the notches of $c$ with those of $c^{*}$ one for one, so $c^{*}$ is happy under $\sigma(a)$ iff $c$ was happy under $a$. Quantify existentially over notches. *Puzzle level.* Quantify universally over pieces. For the set identity, apply the biconditional to $a = \sigma(b)$ and use $\sigma\sigma = \mathrm{id}$. Cardinalities agree because $\sigma$ is injective. $\blacksquare$
The classical statement — "complementing preserves solvability" — is what you get from this by remembering only whether the space is empty. The theorem says the *space itself* travels intact. The algorithm below computes both spaces, checks the transport identity, and returns the parity certificate. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 4. Why the count must be even Put the two spaces side by side inside the same cube — no labels, no bookkeeping about which one a solution came from: $$C(P) = A(P) \cup A(P^{*}).$$ By exact transport, $\sigma$ maps $C(P)$ into itself. And now the crucial, almost embarrassingly simple observation: > **No bit-string is its own complement.** If $n \geq 1$, then $\sigma(a) \neq a$ for every $a$ — look at the first coordinate. So $\sigma$ acts on the finite set $C(P)$ as an involution with **no fixed points**, chopping it into two-element orbits. Hence: > **Parity Theorem.** For every framed puzzle on $n \geq 1$ variables, $|C(P)|$ is even. The same holds for $A(P) \cap A(P^{*})$.
A second proof, with no orbits in it at all Consider $\prod_{a \in C(P)} (-1)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. Pairing each $a$ with $\sigma(a)$ makes the factors cancel telescopically, so the product is $+1$. But the product is also $(-1)^{|C(P)|}$. Hence $(-1)^{|C(P)|}=1$ and the exponent is even. Parity as a signed sum. This is the [sign-reversing involution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Involution_(mathematics)) technique of enumerative combinatorics in its smallest possible instance.
The picture below shows the whole thing at once for $n = 4$: the cube, the matching, the colouring by membership, and — on the right — the single degenerate case where it all breaks. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 5. The surprise: self-duality was never the enemy The result was originally conjectured in a hedged form: *for every framed puzzle **not isomorphic to its own complement**, complementation acts freely, so the combined count is even.* The worry behind the hedge is that a **self-dual** puzzle — one indistinguishable from its mirror — might be a fixed point of the symmetry and escape the law. It is a natural worry. It is also wrong, and the way it is wrong is the most instructive thing here. **Self-duality is a property of puzzles. Freeness is a property of commitments.** The involution $\sigma$ does not act on puzzles at all; it acts on the Boolean cube, where it is free for a reason no puzzle can influence. A self-dual puzzle does not acquire a fixed point — it merely has $A(P^{*}) = A(P)$, so the union collapses onto a single space, on which $\sigma$ *still* acts freely. The conclusion gets **stronger**: > **Self-Dual Parity Theorem.** A framed puzzle on $n \geq 1$ variables with a complement-stable assembly space has an **even number of solutions**. So where does parity actually fail? At $n = 0$. There is exactly one commitment, the empty one; every puzzle is trivially self-complementary because there are no notches to re-mill; the empty puzzle assembles under that commitment; and the combined space has exactly **one** element. Odd. And $\sigma$ genuinely fixes the empty commitment — the unique fixed configuration anywhere in the theory. The hypothesis "$P$ is not isomorphic to its complement" is *unsatisfiable* at $n=0$ and *unnecessary* at $n \geq 1$. It was a dimension filter wearing a symmetry costume.
The three-line proof of the conjecture as originally posed Suppose $P^{*} \neq P$. If $n \geq 1$, apply the Parity Theorem and never use the hypothesis. If $n = 0$, every clause piece is the empty list, so $P^{*} = P$ — contradiction, and the case is vacuous. $\blacksquare$ The proof is worth reading twice: it exhibits the hypothesis as doing exactly one job, and not the job it was hired for.
--- ## 6. From parity to an explicit orbit count Parity is a one-bit shadow. The full statement is a decomposition, and it comes with a *computable* witness. Fix the first variable and define the **polarity gauge** of a set $S$ of commitments: $$\Gamma(S) = \{\, a \in S : a_1 = \texttt{true} \,\}.$$ Because $\sigma$ flips the first coordinate, every orbit $\{a,\sigma(a)\}$ meets $\Gamma(S)$ exactly once. > **Orbit Decomposition.** If $S$ is complement-stable, then $S = \Gamma(S) \sqcup \sigma(\Gamma(S))$, so $|S| = 2\,|\Gamma(S)|$ — and $|\Gamma(S)|$ *is* the number of orbits. Parity is now a corollary with a witness rather than an existence claim. Applied to the whole cube, $|\Gamma| = 2^{n-1}$, bounding the orbits any puzzle can have. {{algorithm:1}}
A curiosity that falls out for free: the sign of complementation Regard $\sigma$ as a permutation of the $2^n$ points of the cube. It is a product of $2^{n-1}$ disjoint transpositions, so $$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = (-1)^{2^{\,n-1}}.$$ For $n = 1$ the exponent is $1$: complementation is an **odd** permutation, a single transposition of a two-point cube. For every $n \geq 2$ the exponent is even and $\sigma$ is an **even** permutation. So the tab–blank symmetry leaves a visible trace in the [sign character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_of_a_permutation) of the symmetric group of the cube in exactly one dimension, and is invisible there ever after. A small fact, but a sharp one: it says the involution's image in $S_{2^n}/A_{2^n} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ is nontrivial only at $n=1$.
--- ## 7. Is parity the *only* constraint? One piece answers the question So far every theorem is a restriction. Does complementation force anything *else* — divisibility by four, say, or bounds away from the extremes? No. And the proof is a construction so simple it fits in a sentence. For a commitment $b$, build the **exclusion piece** $E_b$: one notch per variable, the notch for variable $i$ milled for $\lnot b_i$. Then $E_b$ is happy under $a$ iff some coordinate of $a$ disagrees with $b$ — that is, **iff $a \neq b$**. One piece, one forbidden solution. Now let $S$ be *any* subset of the cube and let $P_S$ consist of $E_b$ for each $b \notin S$. > **Complete Expressiveness Theorem.** $A(P_S) = S$, with $2^n - |S|$ clause pieces. Every subset of the Boolean cube is exactly an assembly space. Framed puzzles are therefore a **complete** constraint language. Two consequences land immediately: * **Single counts are unconstrained.** For every $k \leq 2^n$ some puzzle has exactly $k$ solutions — *odd counts occur*. So parity could never have been a statement about one assembly space. * **The spectrum closes exactly.** Combining freeness with expressiveness: > **Combined Spectrum Theorem.** For $n \geq 1$, a number $m$ is the combined assembly count of some framed puzzle on $n$ variables **if and only if** $m$ is even and $m \leq 2^n$. Freeness supplies "only if"; expressiveness supplies "if". These two algorithms are the two halves: {{algorithm:2}} {{algorithm:3}}
How the "if" direction is built, in three moves To realise a given even $2k \leq 2^n$: 1. Take $k$ points of the gauge (there are $2^{n-1} \geq k$ available). 2. Adjoin their complements. The result $S$ is complement-stable and has exactly $2k$ elements, since gauge points have first coordinate $\texttt{true}$ and their complements $\texttt{false}$, so the two halves are disjoint. 3. Realise $S$ with exclusion pieces. Since $S$ is stable, $A(P_S^{*}) = \sigma(S) = S$, so the combined space *is* $S$. The same construction shows self-dual assembly spaces exist in **every** admissible even size — self-duality is generic, not degenerate. $\blacksquare$
Panel A of the figure below marks, for each $n$, which combined counts are achievable and which are provably impossible. Every square is backed by an explicitly constructed puzzle; every cross by the Parity Theorem. {{visualization:1}} --- ## 8. Exactly how rare is self-duality? Since every subset of the cube is an assembly space, counting assembly spaces is counting subsets — there are $2^{2^n}$ — and counting *self-dual* ones is counting complement-stable subsets. The gauge answers this too: a stable set is determined freely and uniquely by its intersection with the gauge (intersect to go one way, adjoin complements to come back). > **Density Theorem.** For $n \geq 1$ there are exactly $2^{\,2^{\,n-1}}$ complement-stable assembly spaces, and the square of that number is $2^{2^n}$, the total. Self-duality is exactly a **square-root condition**. Panel B above plots it: two straight lines in the doubly-logarithmic scale, one always exactly half the height of the other. For $n=1$: $2$ of $4$. For $n=2$: $4$ of $16$. For $n=3$: $16$ of $256$. For $n=4$: $256$ of $65\,536$. Doubly-exponentially rare in the family, yet present in every admissible size. Rare *and* ubiquitous — the signature of a symmetry class rather than a degeneracy. --- ## 9. Two was never the point Nothing in the argument used the number *two* except in one place: the involution had order two. So replace tab and blank by $d$ distinct **interlock depths**. A variable piece exposes a depth in $\mathbb{Z}/d$, a notch is milled for a required depth, and "deepen every mill by one step" is an order-$d$ symmetry. Everything transports. The depth gauge — commitments whose first variable sits at depth $0$ — meets each shift orbit exactly once, and a shift-stable set of commitments is in explicit bijection with $\mathrm{gauge} \times \mathbb{Z}/d$ via $(g,t) \mapsto g+t$. > **Cyclic Divisibility Theorem.** For $n \geq 1$, the combined assembly space of the $d$ depth-shifts satisfies $|C_d(P)| = d \cdot |\mathrm{gauge}|$, so $d$ divides the combined count. Tab–blank parity is the $d=2$ slice. The constraint on solution counts is not parity as such; it is the **order of the symmetry group acting freely on the configuration space**. Two shapes give evenness; three depths give divisibility by three. Explore it below: set $d$, mill some depth notches, and watch the pooled solution space of all $d$ shifts snap into orbits of length exactly $d$. {{interactive_demo:1}} {{algorithm:4}} --- ## 10. See it all verified at once The first program below runs every result end to end — transport, parity, sharpness at $n=0$, the sign computation, complete expressiveness over *all* $256$ subsets of the three-cube, the exact spectrum, the square-root census, and the cyclic divisibility law with a randomised stress test. {{demo:0}} The second is an **exhaustive** census: for $n = 1,2,3$ it enumerates every framed puzzle built from a bounded catalogue of distinct clause pieces — tens of thousands of them — and checks every theorem on every single one, with no sampling at all. {{demo:1}} --- ## 11. What the flip was really telling us Read backwards, the story is a lesson about **where symmetry lives**. The conjecture placed the symmetry in the puzzle and asked which puzzles were fixed by it. The answer is that the symmetry does not live in the puzzle at all. It lives in the configuration space, where it acts freely for a reason no puzzle can influence, and it acts on assembly spaces only by *transport*. Self-duality is not a fixed point of the action; it is the statement that a particular orbit-stable subset happens to be the solution space of a single puzzle rather than of a complementary pair. That is why the conjecture's hypothesis turned out to exclude a *dimension* rather than a degeneracy, and why the theorem it was guarding is true without it. Once you know the action is free, everything else is counting: $$\text{orbit decomposition} \Rightarrow \text{exact count } 2|\Gamma| \Rightarrow \text{parity} \Rightarrow \text{equinumerosity} \Rightarrow \text{solvability invariance}.$$ Five layers, each a coarser shadow of the one before, all descending from a single sentence — *a bit-string is never its own complement* — and one construction — *one piece can forbid exactly one solution*. Constraint from freeness; expressiveness from a single exclusion piece; and between them, no room left for anything else. Complementation contributes to a framed puzzle exactly **one bit** of global information — the parity of its combined solution count — and, provably, not one bit more.
Open questions this leaves behind * **Minimal piece count.** Our realisation uses $2^n - |S|$ pieces, maximally redundant. Does the minimum equal the minimum number of clauses in a CNF for the indicator of $S$ — and for a complement-stable $S$, is that minimum attained by a *symmetric* set of pieces? The point is that complementation acts on the space of realisations, so symmetrising ought to be free. * **Bounded budgets.** Fix a piece budget. Parity persists but expressiveness does not, so a genuinely new spectrum should appear. What is it? * **Non-abelian mills.** Which finite groups act freely on configuration spaces by re-milling operations, and does $|G| \mid |C|$ persist? Freeness, not commutativity, is what the argument needs. * **Beyond cardinality.** Parity is the only *counting* constraint. Is there structure on the combined space itself — as a graph under [Hamming adjacency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_distance), say — that complementation constrains and cardinality cannot see?
